answer: Use the clock command (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). Set the zone with 'set clock timezone <value>', for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'. The value comes from the fixed named list (International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00] plus Universal-Time-Coordinated); the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see where the time comes from, read 'show clock time-source': ntp means the NE synchronises from NTP, manual means it uses the NE internal clock. The default is manual. 'show clock' also gives current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump, reported as '<time1> to <time2>' with jumps under 10 seconds ignored. If the DNS server is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond.

Yes. node-type is set with 'set ne node-type OADM'; permitted values are ILA, OADM and XPDR. It can only be set or changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, whose default is ILA (G31/G32 default OADM, G42 default XPDR); OADM on G34c is supported from R7.0 onward. To configure node-type OADM the guide requires that no OMS monitoring-mode in the system be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', that is no 'spectrum' (or 'ochm') objects exist in OADM, and that no direction-* exist. Going back the other way, to configure ILA, no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive' (no RD or PAx card can exist), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note that G34c SLTE mode (l0-mode-op slte) is supported only when node-type is ILA, not when it is OADM.

'show ne-function' displays the Network Element generic functions in one listing. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The output enumerates the node's direction and amplifier function objects together, for example on a 1830 GX G30 node: direction-1 through direction-8, amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and the ne-function entry itself.

Use the ntp command (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode): 'set ntp ntp-enabled true' turns on NTP (ntp-enabled is true by default), and 'set ntp ntp-auth-enabled true' requires the synchronisation to be authenticated (ntp-auth-enabled defaults to false). The ntp object is system managed and cannot be manually added or deleted. The third settable attribute is assignment-method, with values manual, dhcp or both, default both, which selects whether the system uses manually configured NTP values, DHCP supplied ones, or both. 'show ntp' returns ntp-enabled, ntp-auth-enabled, assignment-method and ntp-active-server (the currently active NTP server). Authentication also needs keys defined with 'add ntp-key-<key-id>' and bound to a server through the ntp-server auth-key-id attribute.

NTP authentication keys are managed with 'add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]', with matching set, show and delete forms (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). key-type is the hash algorithm used for NTP message digest computation and accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 and md5; there is no default. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8 to 40 characters. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key and takes true or false, defaulting to false. Example: 'add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera'.

Yes. The ntp-server origin attribute is exactly for this: a DHCP configured NTP entry is converted into a manually configured one by changing origin. Run 'set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual'. The permitted values are dhcp (address assigned to this system by a DHCP server) and manual (address manually configured); the default is manual. The server key is the IP address, and IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS domain name are accepted. Other settable attributes on the same object are auth-key-id (uint32 or not-applicable, default not-applicable), label (0..256 characters), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed). 'show ntp-server-<ip-address>' additionally returns oper-state (enabled/disabled, default disabled) and avail-state.

Use 'show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>', for example 'show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218' (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). The key field is reach: an 8-bit shift register of the recent probes with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position, where the value 377 indicates that all the recent probes have been answered. Alongside it you get when (seconds elapsed since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay to the server in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad or none, default none) and condition, whose possible values include sys.peer, reject and candidate.

'restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]' (Operational Mode) takes type cold, warm or shutdown. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes (a cold reboot of an XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, while cold reboot of CHM6, UCM4 and similar is service affecting). warm reboots only the processor of the CHM6, UCM4 and similar and is non service affecting, again regaining connectivity within five minutes (on XMM4 it is non-service affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes). shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. If you do not supply <type>, a warm start is done by default. If you omit <resource-id>, the active node controller card is restarted. The command asks for confirmation unless -f is given, and not all cards support all restart types. Cards can be restarted cold, warm or shutdown, card sub-components cold or warm, and toms cold only.

'set-time' is only applicable when the time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled. If the node is synchronising from NTP it will not accept a hand-set time; check with 'show clock time-source' (values ntp and manual, default manual) and disable synchronisation with 'set ntp ntp-enabled false' if you really need to set it by hand. The syntax is 'set-time [new-time=]<value>' in Operational Mode, with the value in a format derived from ISO 8601 combining date and time, for example 'set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z' where Z is UTC, or a non-UTC offset as in 'set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00'. Read the resulting time back with the 'time' command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used on the set-time command.

Yes: 'status equipment' (Operational mode). The Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with the relevant details, including temperature sensors and power values, plus the list of chassis, the cards per chassis with their subtype, the toms per card, and generic status covering presence or absence, oper state and alarms. The default scope is the entire network element. On a large NE the output can be filtered per chassis by giving the chassis id as the filter, for example 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you either get all chassis or exactly one. Output shows entries such as 'chassis-1 G42 (NC) ok/eqpt discovery temp 25C | power 2.1/4400 W' and fan speeds, with the tick, cross and padlock symbols marking oper-state enabled, oper-state disabled and admin-locked.

Use 'clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>]' in Operational Mode. type factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity; the clear is a secure wipe. The other types are full-wipe, which cleans the entire system and reinstalls software on the controller and line cards and needs a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover, and inactive, which clears the inactive software partition. target may be the whole system or a specific chassis or card AID; with no target the entire system is cleared. restart-behavior is a standard restart by default, or shutdown so the node does not come back up. Limits: factory-reset does not take effect for G30 Optical Carrier-Cards OCC2T and OCC2E, it is supported for the G30 controller card FRCU, and 'clear system factory-reset' with the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. For a simple database wipe use 'clear database' instead. Example: 'clear system factory-reset shutdown'.

Just type 'time'. It is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, takes no parameters, and prints the system's time in combined ISO 8601 date and time form, for example '2020-06-29T22:29:37+00:00'. The time is reported using the system configured timezone. For more detail use 'show clock', which returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, time-source, DST-active and last-time-jump, though note that if DNS is not properly configured show clock can take up to 2 minutes to return.

The 'uptime' command (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, no parameters) displays the system uptime and load average, for example '21:24:09 up 41 days, 15:56, 1 user, load average: 0.10, 0.35, 0.39'. The load average, also called average system load, indicates whether multiple tasks are queued on the system or card. Whether a given number is high or low depends on the number of cores the system has, how many CPUs are integrated into the card, and the load average number itself. The stated rule of thumb is that a load average value is considered high when it is greater than the number of CPUs on the card.

Yes. 'manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<value>' (Operational mode) takes the AID of the object to be switched, and the command warns and asks you to confirm before proceeding: 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. Answer y at the prompt to proceed, or pass -f to force it without confirmation. The examples give 'manual-switchover card-1-3' on a 1830 GX G42 chassis, 'manual-switchover card-1-5' on a G32 chassis and 'manual-switchover card-1-12' on a G34c chassis. For the full procedure the guide points to the 1830 GX Software Management Procedures Guide.

'show protection' displays the node's protection container. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detail beneath it, use 'show protection-group-<name>' for the group attributes (protection-type, pg-state, pg-request, switching-mode, reversion-mode, hold-off-timer, wtr-timer, remaining-wtr, working-pu, protection-pu, reliable-cp and the switch triggers) and 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name>' for each member's state and role.

On protection-group, switching-mode takes unidirectional or bidirectional and defaults to unidirectional. The wait-to-restore timer is wtr-timer: the trigger clearance soaking time before reverting to the working protection unit, measured and set in 1-second steps, with a range of 60..720 seconds and a default of 300. It only applies in revertive mode, and reversion-mode itself takes revertive or non-revertive and defaults to non-revertive, so reversion is off unless you enable it. The related read-only remaining-wtr shows the time left on the WTR timer, range 0..720 seconds, again only applicable in revertive mode. The separate hold-off-timer, the switching trigger soaking time before switching, is set in 1-millisecond steps over the range 0..10000 ms and defaults to 0.

Use the operating command 'protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>' in Operational mode. For a force to the protection path: 'protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection'. operation-type accepts force, lockout, manual and release; switch-target is not needed for the release and lockout operations. -f forces the command without confirmation. Equivalently the group attribute can be driven with 'set protection-group-<name> pg-request forced-to-protection'; pg-request accepts clear, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout and exercise (exercise only for bidirectional SNCP), and defaults to clear.

Use 'show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> [AID] [transport-entity] [state] [role] [alarm-report-control] [label]' in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The state attribute tells you which unit is carrying traffic: it takes active, standby, available or unknown. The role attribute tells you which side of the pair the unit is, working or protection. So the unit whose state is active is the one currently carrying the traffic, and comparing state against role tells you whether you are running on working or on protection. At group level, 'show protection-group-<name> pg-state' and last-switch-trigger give the corresponding group view and the reason for the last switchover.

Most alarms have both an automatic raise criteria and an automatic clear criteria. A very small subset has no clear criteria and instead requires the user to acknowledge and clear them manually. Find which ones with 'show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true'; only entries with can-be-cleared-by-user = true qualify. Clear them with 'clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [[resource=]<value>[,<value>]*]' in Operational mode, for example 'clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL'. -f forces the command without confirmation. This mechanism applies only to system alarms that are not associated with any particular resource but with the system itself, that is system wide or global alarms. Anything else will clear only when its underlying condition goes away.

That is controlled system wide by the alarm-control arc-behavior attribute: 'set alarm-control arc-behavior <leave-alarms|clear-alarms>' (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). leave-alarms, the default, means that when ARC is set to 'inhibit' the current alarms are left in a raised mode; clear-alarms means that when ARC is set to 'inhibit' the current alarms are cleared. Check the setting with 'show alarm-control'. The same command carries alarm-soaking-behavior, which takes automatic (soaking time as defined in the FM profile) or no-soak (certain alarms specified in the FM profile get no soaking time), defaulting to automatic; the OSC LOF alarm instead uses the per-facility user-configurable lof-soak-timer on the PBAx card. Alarms suppressed by ARC can still be seen through 'get-conditions'.

Use 'show alarm-inventory-<alarm-type>', for example 'show alarm-inventory-TIM' or 'show alarm-inventory-MSIM' (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). The alarm-inventory holds all possible alarm types for the system with the static information for each. The attributes returned are alarm-type-description, a description of the alarm type (string 0..128); corrective-action, system provided information on how to correct the situation that triggered the alarm (string 0..256); alarm-category, one of communication, facility, equipment, environmental, processing-error, software, quality-of-service or security; default-severity, the list of possible default severities for that alarm type (critical, major, minor, warning, not-reported, event), which can differ by resource-type; resource-type; and service-affecting, which is indeterminate, sa, nsa or sa-nsa, since the same alarm may be both sa and nsa depending on the resource-type.

Yes, that is exactly what alarm-severity-entry is for: it configures the severity for one particular alarm, keyed by resource type. Use 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>', for example 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor' or 'set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major'. severity accepts critical, event, major, minor, not-reported and warning. resource-type is the card or entity type such as CHM1R, FAN or 1830 GX G31; alarm-type is the abbreviated code such as ADMIN-LOCK or BERSD; direction is na, ingress or egress; location is na, near-end or far-end. Read it back with 'show alarm-severity-entry-...', which also returns the read-only service-affecting value (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Press ? after 'set alarm-severity-entity' to list the available entities. The object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted.

alarm-severity-profile assigns a severity to a whole named profile entry rather than to a single resource-type/alarm-type/direction/location tuple. Its syntax is 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>', with 'show alarm-severity-profile' to display it; press ? after 'set alarm-severity-profile' to list the available profiles. The profile-entry is itself named after the entry it covers, as in 'set alarm-severity-profile alarm-severity-entry-trusted-certificate/CERTIFICATE-EXPIRED severity critical'. By contrast 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>' changes one individual entry, and only that entry, and its show form additionally exposes service-affecting. Both take the same six severity values, both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and both objects are system managed and cannot be manually deleted.

'show current-alarms [number-of-alarms] [last-changed]' gives exactly that, in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. number-of-alarms is the number of currently raised alarms, and last-changed is the timestamp of the last change in the current alarm list, counting either a raise or a clear event. Plain 'show current-alarms' returns both. For a per-severity breakdown alongside other system information, the System dashboard from 'status' (or 'status system') prints a line such as '13 current alarms (1 critical, 5 major, 2 not-reported, 5 minor)'. To list the alarms themselves rather than the count, use 'show alarms'.

Look at the conditions with 'get-conditions' (Operational mode). A condition is an alarm that is not considered current, which happens when the alarm severity is configured as 'not-reported' or 'not-alarmed', when the alarm is suppressed due to alarm correlation, when it is suppressed due to ARC (alarm reporting control), or when it is suppressed due to AINS. The syntax is 'get-conditions [[direction=]<value>] [[resource=]<value>] [[resource-type=]<value>] [[alarm-type=]<value>] [[location=]<value>] [[AID=]<value>]'. direction takes all, na, ingress or egress and defaults to all; location takes all, na, near-end or far-end and also defaults to all; resource, resource-type, alarm-type and AID are free strings with no default. So filter by alarm-type or AID to find the specific alarm you expected.
